expected_evidence: Astronomical: an identifiable, correctly-dated (~12,900 cal BP) supernova remnant within lethal proximity (roughly <50 ly) of the solar system, or a documented progenitor star's absence/disappearance

Astronomical/geological: a cosmogenic isotope spike (14C, 10Be, 36Cl) in ice cores, tree rings, or varved sediments coincident with the Younger Dryas onset, consistent with a gamma-ray-driven ionization/ozone-depletion pulse

Geological: ozone-depletion proxies (NOx/nitrate spikes) in Greenland/Antarctic ice cores, elevated biomass-burning markers (soot, charcoal) from UV-driven wildfire increase, a 'black mat' sedimentary horizon at ~12,900 cal BP across North American sites
Geological: elevated platinum-group elements, nanodiamonds, or magnetic microspherules in the same horizon (often cited in the related impact-hypothesis literature)
Genetic: a demographic bottleneck signature in North American megafaunal and Paleoindian (Clovis-associated) populations dated to this narrow window
Material/archaeological: an abrupt, continent-wide megafaunal extinction horizon and Clovis site abandonment layer stratigraphically tied to the same event

Model-prior: existing scientific literature debating the Younger Dryas impact/supernova hypothesis (e.g., Firestone et al. 2007 and subsequent critiques), which already discusses and largely disfavors a supernova/GRB trigger in favor of other mechanisms
response.rationale: The hypothesis interval (-12000 to -11001) aligns with the Younger Dryas onset, so the 'younger-dryas' detectability row is most applicable. The mechanism (gamma-ray ionization from a nearby supernova) is unusual in that its two strongest evidentiary channels are exactly the ones the table rates as most detectable for this period: astronomical (0.7) and geological (0.65). A supernova close enough to cause biologically significant ionization would leave a remnant still observable today (typical SNRs remain detectable for tens of thousands of years), and it would almost certainly imprint a cosmogenic-isotope and ozone-depletion signal in the well-preserved, continuously sampled Greenland/Antarctic ice-core and varve records spanning this exact interval. These archives are among the best-preserved and most intensively studied paleoclimate proxies available, so relevant evidence — had the event occurred — plausibly would have survived and been found by now. By contrast, textual (0.0), linguistic (0.05), oral_tradition (0.1), and iconographic (0.1) evidence are essentially inapplicable at this depth in time and contribute little either way. Genetic (0.3) and material (0.35) evidence are moderately but not highly detectable, given poor DNA preservation over 13,000 years and incomplete faunal/archaeological sampling. Because the highest-detectability channels (astronomical, geological) are precisely the ones needed to confirm this specific mechanism, and no confirmed proximate-supernova remnant or matching GRB-isotope signature has been reported (model-prior: the literature instead favors either climatic/impact explanations or over-hunting, and the original supernova variant of the hypothesis was largely abandoned/revised toward a cometary-impact framing), the absence of positive evidence here is more likely attributable to the hypothesis being unsupported than to poor preservation or detection limits. I set the aggregate detectability_adjustment at 0.6, reflecting that this hypothesis's most decisive evidence types are well above the period's average detectability, so a low-evidence outcome should weigh more heavily against the hypothesis than a blanket low-detectability excuse would allow.
